heading: What Is an LLM Wiki
content: LLM Wiki is a methodology popularized by Andrej Karpathy for using an LLM to automatically organize raw notes/documents into a structured, interlinked wiki, acting as a persistent memory layer instead of a chat session that resets. It has a 3-layer structure: (1) Raw Sources - original unedited documents the AI reads but never modifies; (2) The Wiki - a folder of AI-generated interlinked Markdown files representing compiled knowledge, owned and updated by the LLM; (3) The Schema - a configuration document (often CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) telling the AI how to structure the wiki, handle new sources, and maintain formatting. Compared to traditional RAG (which searches raw documents on every query), an LLM Wiki compiles and synthesizes knowledge once into a living knowledge base, integrating each new document into the existing network of pages.

heading: Candidate Implementations
content: LLM Wiki is a methodology, not one specific tool, and the original design comes from Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki GitHub Gist (a conceptual framework, not full working code). Community implementations built on top of it include: lucasastorian/llmwiki (full ecosystem - CLI + web app, Chrome extension for clipping pages, native concept-graph viewer, connects to Claude via MCP; widely cited as the most complete/adopted, supports both terminal and web-app usage, and can run fully locally or have its UI hosted separately); nashsu/llm_wiki (cross-platform desktop app for Windows/Mac/Linux with a three-column layout: file tree, chat window, live preview); MehmetGoekce/llm-wiki (bridges AI coding tools like Claude Code into Markdown editors like Obsidian and Logseq, with caching to keep API costs low); eleven-net-cn/llm-wiki-starter (lightweight starter template to bootstrap an empty LLM Wiki directory in one command); green-dalii/obsidian-llm-wiki (Obsidian plugin pairing a CLI agent like Claude Code with the Obsidian app, the 'plugin route' alternative to a standalone web UI).

heading: Mobile-Only Alternative (No Termux / No Computer)
content: Before settling on Termux, a fully mobile workflow was explored: Obsidian (free, iOS/Android, syncs via iCloud/Google Drive) as the visual wiki viewer; Claude or ChatGPT's mobile app/PWA as the AI compiler turning raw text into Markdown wiki pages with [[double-bracket links]]; Markor as a lightweight offline Android Markdown editor used as a fast raw-text inbox when Google Docs/Keep can't open arbitrary plain-text/Markdown/log files. Key practice: keep raw untouched notes in one folder (e.g. 01_Inbox) and AI-generated wiki pages in a separate folder (e.g. 02_Wiki) so source material is never overwritten - Obsidian opens the parent folder and reads both sub-folders, drawing graph links between raw notes and their wiki counterparts. A sync app (Autosync/FolderSync or Google Drive's own sync) keeps a local Android folder mirrored to Google Drive so Obsidian, Termux, and Drive all see the same files. If the Claude client is connected to Google Drive directly, you can skip copy-pasting by attaching the Doc in-chat. Includes two reusable prompts: one that generates a full wiki page from raw text output only as a code block, and a stricter append-only variant that extracts only a bulleted list of [[Wiki Links]] without rewriting or replacing any original text.

heading: Termux Setup: Installing the Open Wiki CLI
content: The 'Open Wiki' CLI referenced is the openwiki npm package (LangChain-agent based), which runs on Node.js. Corrected install (original ran three commands as one unbroken line, which would not execute as intended): `pkg update && pkg upgrade -y`, then `pkg install -y nodejs git`, then `npm install -g openwiki`. Usage: navigate to your repo folder and run `openwiki --init`. By default it expects an API key (e.g. Anthropic) in the environment; to use a local model instead, point it at your local server's base URL. The openwiki npm package name and its LangChain/agent-oriented description were confirmed against the public npm registry (latest version 0.0.2, maintained by basproul).

heading: Running a Local LLM API in Termux
content: Two ways to run a local OpenAI-compatible LLM API in Termux. Option A: llama.cpp compiled from source (there is no prebuilt 'llama-cpp' Termux package, contrary to the original text's `pkg install llama-cpp` - it must be built): `pkg update && pkg upgrade -y`, `pkg install -y git cmake clang make`, `git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp`, `cd llama.cpp`, `cmake -B build`, `cmake --build build --config Release -j"$(nproc)"`. Then run the compiled binary directly (not a bare `llama-server` on PATH): `./build/bin/llama-server -m /sdcard/Download/your-model.Q4_K_M.gguf -c 4096 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`, exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:8080/v1 and http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions. Option B: Ollama, which IS a real installable Termux package: `pkg install -y ollama` then `ollama serve &` (must be started manually/backgrounded, unlike a desktop install), followed by `ollama pull <model>` / `ollama run <model>`. Verify either server with a curl POST to /v1/chat/completions from a second Termux session while the server runs in the first. Model guidance: Snapdragon 8 Gen2/3/Elite devices with 12-16GB RAM can run 4B-9B GGUF quantized models at interactive speeds (community-reported, unverified benchmarks); smaller/faster options include Phi-3-mini and Qwen 2.5/3.5 4B quants, larger/smarter-for-code options include Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B / Qwen3 8B-9B quants. Reducing the -c context size (e.g. 8192 to 2048-4096) reduces RAM usage under memory pressure. A toggle script (toggle_qwen.sh) can switch between a small/fast and large/smart model server without retyping paths; corrected to invoke ./build/bin/llama-server instead of a bare, non-existent llama-server binary.

heading: Repo Structure for Multi-Project Setups
content: To avoid one giant unorganized folder when the wiki feeds multiple downstream projects (e.g. separate GGUF/ONNX/TFLite-targeted codebases), use a hub-and-spoke layout with the wiki pulled in as a Git submodule or subtree rather than copy-pasted: a 00_Master_Wiki folder as the central source of truth, with each project fork containing its own docs/core_wiki read-only copy. To link as a submodule: `cd /sdcard/AI_Projects/Project_Fork_A`, `git init`, `git submodule add /sdcard/AI_Projects/00_Master_Wiki docs/core_wiki`. To pull in as a subtree instead (files land directly in the repo, no .gitmodules pointer): `git subtree add --prefix=docs/wiki ~/my-master-wiki main --squash`. Both commands are valid Git syntax as given in the source material; git subtree add requires the source path to itself be a Git repository with the referenced branch.

heading: PDF / Docs to JSONL (Docling)
content: Docling (IBM) turns PDFs/long documents into a fast, machine-searchable cache: it parses layout including tables and multi-column text, and emits both a human-readable Markdown copy and a machine-readable JSON Lines (.jsonl) file with one JSON object per chunk plus metadata, intended for fast line-by-line retrieval instead of re-parsing a whole document per query. Install (corrected from a single broken line): `pkg install -y python` then `pip install docling`. Docling has heavy dependencies (PyTorch-based layout models) and pure-Termux installs can fail with native build errors on Android arm64; if so, install proot-distro and run a Debian/Ubuntu userland inside Termux first, then install Docling there: `pkg install -y proot-distro`, `proot-distro install debian`, `proot-distro login debian`, then inside the Debian shell `apt update && apt install -y python3 python3-pip` and `pip install docling`. The .jsonl output is plain, uncompressed, line-delimited JSON - readable but not meant for humans; keep the Markdown copy for reading in Obsidian and let tooling consume the .jsonl for fast search.

heading: Extracting URLs from a Chat Log
content: To pull a clean, deduplicated list of URLs from a raw exported chat transcript using only built-in Termux tools: `grep -o 'https\?://[^"]\+' chat.txt > urls_only.txt`, or deduplicated with `grep -o 'https\?://[^" ]\+' chat_log.txt | sort -u > clean_urls.txt`. Both rely on GNU grep's \? / \+ basic-regex extensions (supported by Termux's grep) and run correctly once PDF line-wrap escaping artifacts are removed; sort -u removes duplicate lines. To convert a public webpage or already-public chat share-link into a clean PDF or Markdown copy, the referenced tools are PrintFriendly / Microlink (URL to PDF) and Firecrawl / Jina AI Reader (URL to Markdown). These tools cannot scrape a logged-in AI chat UI directly - first create a public share link from inside the chat app's Share menu, or export/copy the transcript to a local file and process it with the grep commands above instead.

heading: Voice I/O in Termux: Hardware Bridge, TTS, STT
content: Standalone STT/TTS Python models tend to hang or get killed in Termux because Android's security sandbox blocks raw microphone/audio-thread access from a terminal app. The reliable path uses Android's native voice engine through the separate Termux:API companion app (install from the same source as Termux itself, F-Droid recommended over Play Store) instead of a standalone model. Setup: `pkg update && pkg upgrade -y`, `pkg install -y termux-api`, then in Android Settings > Apps > Termux:API grant Microphone, Storage, and unrestricted background/battery permissions. Text-to-speech: `termux-tts-speak "text"`, or pipe file/command output directly, e.g. `cat docs/core_wiki/Project_Notes.md | termux-tts-speak`. Speech-to-text: `termux-speech-to-text` prints transcribed text to the terminal after a beep; redirect to a file with `termux-speech-to-text >> /sdcard/My_Drive_Sync/01_Inbox/voice_log.txt`. Voice round-trip through a local LLM: capture text with termux-speech-to-text, then send it to the local /v1/chat/completions endpoint and speak back the reply.

heading: Voice Round-Trip Through a Local LLM (JSON-safety fix)
content: The original voice-to-LLM pipeline built the JSON request body by directly interpolating "$(termux-speech-to-text)" inside a hand-written JSON string, and parsed the reply with a fragile grep -o '"content":"[^"]*' | cut -d'"' -f4 chain. If the spoken text contains a double quote, backslash, or newline, both the request body and the parse step break. Corrected version: `TEXT=$(termux-speech-to-text)` then `curl -s http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "$(jq -n --arg t \"$TEXT\" '{model:\"local-model\", messages:[{role:\"user\", content:$t}]}')" | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content' | termux-tts-speak`. This uses jq -n to safely construct the JSON request and jq -r '.choices[0].message.content' to reliably extract the reply; requires `pkg install -y jq`.

heading: 100% Offline Alternative: whisper.cpp
content: For STT with no reliance on Android's built-in engine (fully offline, no Google/Samsung services), compile whisper.cpp directly. The original install command was broken - it ran `pkg install clang cmake make wave-play git clone https://github.com cd whisper.cpp` as one line; 'wave-play' is not a real Termux package, and the git clone URL was truncated (missing the actual repo path). Corrected: `pkg update && pkg upgrade -y`, `pkg install -y clang cmake make git ffmpeg`, `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp.git`, `cd whisper.cpp`, `cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_NO_OPENMP=ON`, `cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"`, `bash ./models/download-ggml-model.sh base.en`. The -DGGML_NO_OPENMP=ON flag avoids a thread-crash issue on Android that the original text alluded to but didn't name. To record and transcribe manually, the original recorded to voice.amr and fed it straight into ./main -f voice.amr, but termux-microphone-record's encoders (aac/amr_wb/amr_nb/opus) don't produce whisper.cpp's required format, and whisper.cpp needs 16kHz mono 16-bit PCM WAV input, not amr/aac directly. Corrected: `termux-microphone-record -f /sdcard/voice.m4a -l 10`, `ffmpeg -i /sdcard/voice.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le /sdcard/voice.wav`, `./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-base.en.bin -f /sdcard/voice.wav` (the compiled binary in current whisper.cpp builds is build/bin/whisper-cli, not ./main, which was renamed in a later release).

heading: Diagnosing Unidentified Model Files
content: If a downloaded voice/model file's format is unclear (missing or ambiguous extension), inspect it directly: `ls -lh /sdcard/Download/ | grep -iE 'onnx|txt|bin|json|pth'`, `pkg install -y file`, `file /sdcard/Download/your_model_filename_here`. Interpreting file's output: ONNX / serialized Protocol Buffer means a raw ONNX runtime model loadable directly with onnxruntime; ASCII text likely means a plain-text token/phoneme dictionary, confirmable with `head /sdcard/Download/tokens.txt`; data / PyTorch zip archive means a raw PyTorch (.pth) checkpoint or generic tensor binary (.bin) needing a full PyTorch runtime or dedicated C++ loader, not just onnxruntime. Files created inside Termux's home directory (~) live in a private sandbox that Android apps cannot browse; search for 'lost' files and move them to shared storage with `find ~ -type f \( -iname "*kokoro*" -o -iname "*cocoro*" \)` then `mkdir -p /sdcard/Download/shared_models` and `cp ~/path/to/found/file /sdcard/Download/shared_models/`. A minimal, explicitly non-functional Python skeleton (loads an ONNX session, takes text in, writes a placeholder silent WAV out) illustrates the plumbing for driving a split Kokoro model.onnx + tokens.txt pair, but real tokenization/inference still needs to be filled in. Prebuilt TTS apps (e.g. VoxSherpa-style apps) often require models in a specific bundled format (e.g. Piper: single .onnx file plus same-named .onnx.json config) and may refuse to import a differently-structured raw Kokoro export through their manual import UI; prefer an app's own in-app model catalog download over manually importing raw split files when both are available.
